reading.body:
Nonprofit AI adoption is measured by sector research organizations, not a real-time registry, and the binding constraint is governance capacity rather than compute or power.

The seven sources split the problem into distinct angles. CEP and NTEN survey how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. The AI Equity Project tracks access and training gaps. Candid tracks grantmaking for AI adoption and technology infrastructure. Census BTOS includes nonprofit-heavy service sectors in its adoption series, and Stanford HAI reports macro social impact. No single entity maintains a real-time registry.

The practical uses named are grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets. Because governance capacity is the stated constraint, AI scaling in this sector is limited by oversight and policy adoption, not by access to compute or grid power. The data does not support a compute or power constraint for nonprofits.

The data does not provide adoption rates, budget figures, or compute and power requirements. It identifies who publishes sector research, not how many nonprofits have deployed AI or what infrastructure they use.

summary: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery are the practical uses; governance capacity is the constraint. No single entity keeps a real-time registry of nonprofit AI adoption - coverage comes from sector research organizations, and this page names the ones that actually publish it.

analysis.body:
The closest official measure for this sector comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks firms whether they used AI in the last two weeks. For Other services, NAICS 81, the category that includes grantmaking and civic organizations, 15.0% answered yes in the latest period, against 13.7% in the prior period. The Bureau notes that some values in the series are suppressed, and the category is broader than nonprofits alone, so the figure is a benchmark rather than a nonprofit-specific count. The survey first asked about AI in September 2023.

On what the technology is actually used for, Candid describes the most concrete shift in the harvested material: donors are increasingly using AI tools to research causes and charities, which means many won't ever see a nonprofit's website, donation page, or newsletter. That reframes AI as a discovery and fundraising problem before it is an operations problem. The Center for Effective Philanthropy's sector research, including its AI-focused reporting, examines how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications, though the page harvested here shows little beyond the organization's research role and a participatory grantmaking model. NTEN runs regular sector-wide research on technology investment, digital maturity, and AI policy adoption among nonprofits.

The supply side of the sector is thin and mostly not infrastructure. The World of AI's own catalogue lists four individually verified organizations, two nonprofits and two open-source foundations, and states plainly that none are infrastructure builders in the compute or power sense. LMSYS stewards Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform used to benchmark model quality, which the page argues matters because model comparison sits outside the commercial incentives of the labs being evaluated. Khan Academy is described as an end-user of AI capability in education rather than a producer of it, and the Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with. The same page is explicit about what its data does not cover: no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights. Its notes confirm organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.

The access gap is where the sector's own organizations concentrate their language. The AI Equity Project describes building structured learning pathways and intergenerational programs, turning public libraries and community spaces into interactive learning environments that bring senior citizens and student volunteers together around practical AI tools. It operates as a global network providing standardized technical curricula and training assets to underrepresented communities, and runs the International AI for Impact Challenge, where top participants secure engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advisement. NTEN frames the same problem as inequity within organizations and within the sector, and offers an Equity Guide, professional certificates, scholarships for those with tight finances, and recognition for open source tools that nonprofit and advocacy groups can use.

Evidence on return on investment is largely absent from the material here. Candid is described as tracking grantmaking trends, including funding directed toward AI adoption and technology infrastructure, but the harvested page reports no dollar figures or outcomes. Stanford HAI's AI Index is listed among the site's sources as the citable macro series on AI's social impact and implementation across mission-driven and public-sector organizations, yet no figures from it appear in the harvested text. The Center for Effective Philanthropy and NTEN are both described as conducting sector research, but the pages captured do not report measured results. On ROI, the sources are silent, and that silence is itself the finding.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material points to two constraints rather than one. The first is budget: the coverage note for this sector describes grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets. The second is governance capacity, which the same note names as the binding constraint, and which the ecosystem catalogue reinforces by noting that its entries confirm structure and status but not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail. The Census Bureau figure of 15.0% gives a comparison point for how common adoption has become in the broader services category, and Candid's observation about donors researching with AI suggests the cost of doing nothing is partly a visibility problem. Beyond that, the sources describe intent, access work, and cataloguing more than they describe results.

https://cep.org/.brief: The page from the Center for Effective Philanthropy features an article by Kevin Bolduc, who is identified as vice president of assessment and advisory services. The article’s title asks how one collaborative’s movement-led participatory model makes a difference for grantees. The harvested text does not include any further details or findings.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid says it provides comprehensive grants and nonprofit data to help users find funding, research nonprofits, and connect with funders. The page also notes that donors are increasingly using AI tools to research causes and charities. According to the text, this means many donors will never see a nonprofit's website, donation page, or newsletter.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.

https://theaiequityproject.org/.brief: The AI Equity Project reports that it develops structured educational routes and cross-generational initiatives aimed at making AI usable, ethical, and practical for every community. It says it converts public libraries and local community venues into hands-on learning settings where older adults and student volunteers jointly try out practical AI tools. The organization also describes a worldwide network that supplies standardized technical curricula and training materials to underrepresented groups, with support structures meant to ensure each student directly helps deploy machine learning architectures. Its International AI for Impact Challenge asks engineering candidates to propose operational algorithms for real-world issues, and top entrants receive engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advice.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: This page catalogues four individually verified organisations ,  two nonprofits and two open-source foundations ,  whose roles touch AI tooling and evaluation, though the page states none are infrastructure builders in the compute-or-power sense. It describes LMSYS as the most directly AI-central entry, stewarding the Chatbot Arena evaluation platform used by the wider AI community to benchmark model quality, while characterising Khan Academy as an end-user of AI in education rather than a producer of it. The Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation are described as stewards of creative software that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with, with missions the page says predate and are not defined by AI. The page also flags what its data omits: no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights publicly, with the notes confirming only organisational structure and nonprofit status rather than funding scale, compute access or governance detail.
